extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / American wartime public
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-1943 newspaper article reporting on Allied military developments (Tunisian victory), wartime administration issues (prisoner handling, WAACs recruiting), and post-war policy commentary. Aimed at informing the general public about military, legislative and policy developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geneva Prisoners of War Convention (1929) — permitted work and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 1929 Geneva Prisoners of War Convention, prisoners may perform farm work but are forbidden to perform work that aids the war effort of their own countries; conditions of work must conform to the Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states the convention 'permits farm work but forbids work aiding the war effort against their own countries.' It notes that utilization of war prisoners must conform to these rules and that work done for the account of private persons or public administrations has to meet Convention conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geneva Convention — wages and payment rules for POW labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners are entitled to wages for labor; payment for labor shall be settled according to agreements between belligerents or by rates in force for soldiers doing the same work (or a rate in harmony with such rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes that wages are to be fixed by agreement between belligerents or according to national army rates; examples/numbers in the reporting include an approximate planned payment of about 80 cents daily for labor plus a 10-cent daily allowance for toilet necessities and tobacco, and that officers (not worked outside camps) receive $20 to $40 a month in amounts related to their rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions and special rules for officers and prisoners in camps
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers are not to be worked outside prison camps proper; prisoners held in certain contexts (e.g., those with dependents) may be handled differently under internment systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article indicates officers receive supplemental amounts ($20–$40 monthly) and highlights that the Convention and subsequent internment arrangements create differentiated handling (e.g., for heads of families or married men versus single men). It also mentions logistical arrangements for shipping/interment (facilities in Canada, shipment to America/England).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative proposal to place WAACs 'in' the Army (rather than 'with') — benefits and status
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill reported favorably by the House Military Affairs Committee would place WAACs 'in' the Army rather than 'with' it, thereby securing army benefit payments and other military benefits for women's corps members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage explains the practical effect: placement 'in' the Army secures army benefit payments. The article also provides recruiting context: authorized strength 150,000, current recruited ~60,000 (less than half), and cited requests/demand suggesting a need for up to 500,000 WAACs; recruiting secrecy and press campaigns were described as measures to boost enlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Furlough extension policy for new inductees
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department extended the furlough period for new inductees from 7 days to 14 days (in some parts of the country immediately), to give men time to wind up civilian affairs before report for active military duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states the extension would be effective immediately in some parts and delayed in others due to administrative transition difficulties; commanding generals of service commands were ordered to make the extension as soon as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft/induction timing for fathers (administrative target)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans or proposals discussed that draft/induction schedules for certain categories (e.g., fathers) could begin by specific target dates (example mentioned: 'begin inducting fathers by Aug. 1').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This appears as a policy timetable in reporting about manpower planning; presented as a likely or proposed change rather than a guaranteed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-war international-organization objectives (Landon's propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of propositions for organizing post-war international affairs: (1) an interim world council of the United Nations to handle punishment of the guilty, disarmament, famine relief, responsible governments and peace machinery; (2) U.S. indication of desirability of some permanent international organization; (3) recognition that some international concerns may be handled on a regional basis; (4) vesting world/regional organizations with responsibilities to prevent conflicts; (5) prioritizing the Western Hemisphere's concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as policy criteria/principles proposed by Alf Landon for U.S. post-war objectives. The article reports his caution about secret covenants and his argument for frank public discussion of foreign policy; it also highlights his insistence on preventing government-controlled news dissemination around such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle opposing government control of news (press freedom standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A normative standard articulated: foreign policy and international conferences should not be communicated under a government-controlled news monopoly; free discussion by the public and press is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes Landon and references concerns that government-controlled news caused harms in earlier conferences; he urges that decisions affecting many lives should not be imparted without opportunity for public scrutiny and that secret covenants are dangerous precedents.
